code.title: Cosine vs Euclidean: direction versus length
code.python:
import math

def dot(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))

def cosine(a, b):
    na, nb = math.sqrt(dot(a, a)), math.sqrt(dot(b, b))
    if na == 0 or nb == 0:      # zero vector has no direction
        return None
    return dot(a, b) / (na * nb)

def euclid(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

short = [1, 2, 0]
long_ = [10, 20, 0]    # same direction, 10x longer
other = [0, 1, 3]
print("a =", short, " b =", long_, " c =", other)
# Cosine ignores length; Euclidean does not
print("cos(a,b) =", round(cosine(short, long_), 3), " euclid(a,b) =", round(euclid(short, long_), 3))
print("cos(a,c) =", round(cosine(short, other), 3), " euclid(a,c) =", round(euclid(short, other), 3))
print("cos(a,zero) =", cosine(short, [0, 0, 0]))
# Unit vectors: |u-v|^2 == 2 - 2cos
u = [x / math.sqrt(dot(short, short)) for x in short]
v = [x / math.sqrt(dot(other, other)) for x in other]
print("check:", round(euclid(u, v) ** 2, 4), "==", round(2 - 2 * cosine(short, other), 4))

followUps:
The result is undefined, so you must decide what to return. A zero vector has length 0, and cosine divides by that length, which gives 0/0.

Common choices are to return 0 (no similarity), return None or raise an error, or add a tiny epsilon such as 1e-12 to the denominator. In an embedding pipeline an all-zero vector usually means empty or failed input, so I filter or flag it rather than silently matching it with everything.

Not quite: cosine distance (1 minus cosine similarity) breaks the triangle inequality, so it is not a true metric.

Example: A=(1,0), B=(1,1), C=(0,1). d(A,B)=1-0.707=0.293, d(B,C)=0.293, but d(A,C)=1, which is more than 0.293+0.293=0.586. The fix is angular distance, arccos(cos), which is a true metric. In practice, ranking neighbours works fine with cosine distance.

They normalise so that a fast dot product equals cosine similarity. If every stored vector has length 1, cosine reduces to the plain dot product, with no division at query time.

It also lets one index serve dot-product, cosine and Euclidean ranking, because for unit vectors |a-b|^2 = 2 - 2cos. The cost is a one-off O(d) division per vector at insert time, which pays for itself on every query across millions of vectors.

code.title: 2x3 times 3x2 matrix product with cost count
code.python:
def matmul(A, B):
    m, n, p = len(A), len(B), len(B[0])
    assert len(A[0]) == n, "inner dimensions must match"
    C = [[0] * p for _ in range(m)]
    mults = 0
    for i in range(m):              # each output cell is one dot product
        for j in range(p):
            for k in range(n):
                C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j]
                mults += 1
    return C, mults

A = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
B = [[7, 8], [9, 10], [11, 12]]
C, mults = matmul(A, B)
print("A (2x3) =", A)
print("B (3x2) =", B)
print("A@B (2x2) =", C, "multiplications:", mults)
D, _ = matmul(B, A)
print("B@A (3x3) =", D, "-> different shape, not commutative")
# Cost m*n*p; for square N x N this is N^3
for N in (10, 100):
    print("N =", N, "multiplications =", N ** 3)

followUps:
No, in general A times B is not equal to B times A.

With a 2x3 and a 3x2, A@B is 2x2 but B@A is 3x3, so they are not even the same shape. Even for square matrices the results usually differ: [[1,2],[3,4]] times [[0,1],[1,0]] gives [[2,1],[4,3]], while the reverse order gives [[3,4],[1,2]]. It is associative, (AB)C = A(BC), and distributes over addition, and those two properties are what you rely on in practice.

Because every output cell is an independent dot product, so thousands can be computed at the same time.

A GPU has thousands of simple cores and very high memory bandwidth, which is exactly what this regular, predictable pattern needs. For two 1000x1000 matrices there are 1,000,000 independent cells, each needing 1000 multiply-adds. A CPU does these a few at a time, a GPU does huge batches at once. Neural nets are mostly matrix multiplies, so GPUs speed up training a great deal.

It is (n, n), where n is the sequence length: one score for every query-key pair.

Q is (n, d) and Kt is (d, n), so (n, d) times (d, n) gives (n, n). For n=4096 that is about 16.8 million scores per head, which is why attention memory and compute grow quadratically with context length. Entry (i, j) says how much token i should attend to token j.

code.title: Naive vs stable softmax and temperature
code.python:
import math

def naive(z):
    e = [math.exp(x) for x in z]
    s = sum(e)
    return [x / s for x in e]

def stable(z, T=1.0):
    z = [x / T for x in z]
    m = max(z)                      # subtract max: largest exponent becomes 0
    e = [math.exp(x - m) for x in z]
    s = sum(e)                      # s >= 1, never overflows
    return [x / s for x in e]

z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]
print("logits", z)
print("naive ", [round(p, 3) for p in naive(z)])
print("stable", [round(p, 3) for p in stable(z)])
big = [1000.0, 1001.0, 999.0]
print("big logits", big)
try:
    print("naive ", naive(big))
except OverflowError as err:
    print("naive  fails:", err)
print("stable", [round(p, 3) for p in stable(big)])
for T in (0.1, 1.0, 10.0):
    print("T =", T, [round(p, 3) for p in stable(z, T)])

followUps:
As T goes to 0 the output becomes one-hot on the largest logit (greedy), and as T goes to infinity it becomes uniform.

With logits [2,1,0.1]: T=0.1 gives about [1.00, 0.00, 0.00], T=1 gives [0.66, 0.24, 0.10], T=10 gives [0.37, 0.33, 0.30]. Dividing by a small T exaggerates the gaps between logits, dividing by a large T shrinks them to nearly nothing. T=0 itself is implemented as argmax, because dividing by zero is not allowed.

The gradient with respect to the logits is simply (p - y): predicted probabilities minus the one-hot true label.

Example: p=[0.7,0.2,0.1] and true class 0 gives y=[1,0,0], so the gradient is [-0.3, 0.2, 0.1]. It pushes the true logit up and the others down in proportion to the error. This clean form is why softmax and cross-entropy are fused in one function; it is also more numerically stable than computing them separately.

Softmax picks one class out of several that compete, sigmoid scores each class independently.

Softmax outputs sum to 1, so use it for single-label problems (one digit from 0-9). Sigmoid gives each output its own 0-1 probability, so use it for multi-label problems (a photo can be both 'beach' and 'dog'). For two classes they are equivalent: sigmoid(z) equals softmax over the logits [z, 0].

code.title: Bayes rule for a rare disease test
code.python:
sens = 0.99          # P(+ | sick)
fpr = 0.05           # P(+ | healthy)
prior = 0.001        # P(sick)

def posterior(prior):
    true_pos = sens * prior
    false_pos = fpr * (1 - prior)
    return true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos)

p1 = posterior(prior)
print("P(sick | +) =", round(p1, 4))
# Natural frequencies out of 100000 people
n = 100000
sick = n * prior
print("sick:", sick, "true positives:", sick * sens)
print("healthy:", n - sick, "false positives:", round((n - sick) * fpr, 1))
# A second independent positive test: the posterior becomes the new prior
p2 = posterior(p1)
print("after 2nd positive test:", round(p2, 4))
# Effect of the base rate
for pr in (0.001, 0.01, 0.1):
    print("prior", pr, "-> P(sick|+) =", round(posterior(pr), 3))

followUps:
It rises sharply, because two independent positives multiply the odds. In this example from about 1.9% to about 28%.

Use the first posterior as the new prior: 0.99x0.0194 / (0.99x0.0194 + 0.05x0.9806) = 0.0192/0.0682 = 0.28. A third positive would take it to about 88%. Each positive result multiplies the odds by the likelihood ratio 0.99/0.05 = 19.8, so repeated testing is the standard way to confirm a rare condition.

Sensitivity is recall, and the 'chance you are sick given a positive' is precision.

In the 100,000-person example there are 99 true positives, 1 missed case and 4,995 false positives. Recall = 99/100 = 99%, but precision = 99/(99+4995) = about 1.9%. A model can have excellent recall and terrible precision when the positive class is rare, which is why accuracy alone is misleading on imbalanced data.

Then multiplying the probabilities overstates the evidence, and the posterior after two positives will be too high.

If both tests fail for the same reason (say the same cross-reacting substance), a false positive on test 1 makes a false positive on test 2 much more likely than 5%. With perfect correlation the second test adds no information and the answer stays near 1.9%. You then need the joint probability P(++|healthy), not the product 0.05x0.05.

code.title: Broadcasting shape rule and the (100,) vs (100,1) bug

followUps:
An accidental broadcast can create a huge array. Two vectors of length N can turn into an N x N matrix.

With N=100,000 float64 values, the result has 10^10 cells, about 80 GB, versus 800 KB for the vector. NumPy often allocates that result before you notice. It is the same reason all-pairs distance with broadcasting is only practical for moderate N. I process in chunks or use a dedicated function when N is large.

keepdims=True keeps the reduced axis with length 1 instead of removing it, so the result still broadcasts correctly against the original.

For x of shape (3,4), x.sum(axis=1) has shape (3,), which does not line up with x, while x.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) has shape (3,1). So x / x.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) divides each row by its own sum. Without keepdims you get an error or, worse, silent wrong results.

Add a size-1 axis to each side so the difference broadcasts to a 3D array, then reduce.

For X of shape (n, d): diff = X[:, None, :] - X[None, :, :] has shape (n, n, d), and dist = np.sqrt((diff**2).sum(axis=-1)) is (n, n). Cost is O(n^2 d) time and O(n^2 d) memory for the diff, so for large n use the identity |a-b|^2 = |a|^2 + |b|^2 - 2a.b, which needs only an (n, n) matrix.

code.title: Scale with train statistics only
code.python:
import math

def fit(xs):
    mean = sum(xs) / len(xs)
    std = math.sqrt(sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in xs) / len(xs))
    return mean, std or 1.0         # guard against zero std

def transform(xs, mean, std):
    return [(x - mean) / std for x in xs]

train = [20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
test = [25, 70]
mean, std = fit(train)              # learn ONLY from training data
print("train stats: mean =", mean, " std =", round(std, 3))
print("train scaled:", [round(v, 2) for v in transform(train, mean, std)])
print("test  scaled (train stats):", [round(v, 2) for v in transform(test, mean, std)])
# Leaky version: statistics from train + test together
lm, ls = fit(train + test)
print("leaky stats: mean =", round(lm, 2), " std =", round(ls, 3))
print("test  scaled (leaky):", [round(v, 2) for v in transform(test, lm, ls)])
print("constant column ->", fit([5, 5, 5]))

followUps:
No. Decision trees (and random forests, gradient boosting) split on thresholds, and a threshold is unaffected by rescaling.

Whether you split on age < 30 or on the z-score of age < -0.5, the same rows land on each side. Linear models, neural nets, k-NN, SVM and k-means do care, because they use distances or gradients. I still avoid unneeded work but would scale if the same pipeline also feeds a model that needs it.

A new category must be handled by a rule you chose in advance, because the encoder has never seen it.

Common options are an 'unknown' bucket, an all-zeros one-hot row, or hashing. For example, if training had colors {red, blue} and production sees 'green', a one-hot encoder with ignore-unknown outputs [0,0]. A crash in production is the worst outcome, so I configure this behaviour explicitly and monitor how often unknowns appear.

Population std divides by n and sample std divides by n-1. Use the sample version when your data is a sample of a bigger group.

For [20,30,40,50,60]: squared deviations sum to 1000, so population std is sqrt(1000/5)=14.14 and sample std is sqrt(1000/4)=15.81. For scaling features, either is fine if you use it consistently in training and inference. The difference is tiny for large n. NumPy defaults to ddof=0, pandas to ddof=1, which is a classic mismatch.

code.title: Group-by average with a dict, checked against SQL
code.python:
rows = [("a", 10), ("b", 4), ("a", 20), ("c", 7), ("b", 6), ("a", 30)]
print("rows:", rows)

def group_avg(rows):
    acc = {}                         # key -> [sum, count]
    for k, v in rows:                # one pass: O(N) time
        s = acc.setdefault(k, [0, 0])
        s[0] += v
        s[1] += 1
    return {k: s / c for k, (s, c) in acc.items()}   # O(K) space

print("avg per key:", group_avg(rows))

# Same idea with a tuple key (multi-column group by)
rows2 = [("a", "x", 1), ("a", "y", 3), ("a", "x", 5)]
acc = {}
for k1, k2, v in rows2:
    s = acc.setdefault((k1, k2), [0, 0])
    s[0] += v
    s[1] += 1
print("two keys:", {k: s / c for k, (s, c) in acc.items()})

# SQL equivalent: SELECT k, AVG(v) FROM t GROUP BY k
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("create table t(k text, v int)")
db.executemany("insert into t values (?,?)", rows)
print("sql:", db.execute("select k, avg(v) from t group by k order by k").fetchall())

followUps:
Sort the rows within each group by the value, then keep the first N, or use a heap of size N per group.

In SQL: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY v DESC), then keep rn <= N. In pandas: df.sort_values('v', ascending=False).groupby('k').head(N). With a size-N heap per group the cost is O(rows x log N) instead of a full sort of O(rows x log rows).

Process it in chunks and keep only the running state per group, not the rows.

For an average, the state is [sum, count] per key, so you read the file in pieces, update the dict, and discard each piece. This needs O(K) memory for K groups. If K is also huge, partition by hash of the key into files or machines (map-reduce style) so each partition's groups fit in memory, then combine the partial sums.

WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, HAVING filters whole groups after the aggregate is computed.

Example: SELECT k, AVG(v) FROM t WHERE v > 0 GROUP BY k HAVING AVG(v) > 10. Rows with v<=0 are dropped first, then groups whose average is 10 or less are dropped. You cannot use an aggregate like AVG in WHERE because it does not exist yet at that stage.

code.title: Temperature reshapes token probabilities
code.python:
import math, random

def probs(logits, T):
    z = [x / T for x in logits]
    m = max(z)
    e = [math.exp(x - m) for x in z]
    s = sum(e)
    return [x / s for x in e]

tokens = ["the", "a", "cat", "zebra"]
logits = [3.0, 2.0, 1.0, -1.0]
for T in (0.2, 1.0, 2.0):
    p = probs(logits, T)
    print("T =", T, {t: round(x, 3) for t, x in zip(tokens, p)})

random.seed(7)                       # a seed makes sampling repeatable
for T in (0.2, 1.0, 2.0):
    p = probs(logits, T)
    draws = random.choices(tokens, weights=p, k=1000)
    counts = {t: draws.count(t) for t in tokens}
    print("T =", T, "1000 samples:", counts)
print("greedy (T->0) always picks:", tokens[logits.index(max(logits))])

followUps:
Both limit which tokens can be sampled. Top-k keeps a fixed number of the best tokens, top-p keeps as many as needed to reach a total probability.

With probabilities [0.5,0.3,0.1,0.05,0.05]: top-k=2 keeps 2 tokens; top-p=0.9 keeps the first three (0.5+0.3+0.1=0.9). Top-p adapts: when the model is confident it keeps only 1 or 2 tokens, when it is unsure it keeps many. Renormalise the kept probabilities, then sample.

A seed makes the random draws repeatable, so you can reproduce a result for debugging, tests or comparing two prompts.

With T above 0 the sample is random: the same prompt can give different answers each run. Fixing the seed (where the API supports it) gives the same draws given the same model and settings. It is not a guarantee of identical output across model versions or hardware, so I also log the prompt, parameters and output.

Higher temperature makes unlikely tokens more probable, which increases the chance of invented or inconsistent statements.

At T=0.2 the top token with 66% at T=1 might get 99%, so it is nearly always chosen; at T=2 a 1% token rises to about 6%. Low temperature does not remove hallucination, though: if the model's top choice is wrong, greedy decoding repeats it confidently. Grounding with retrieved sources and checking facts matters more than temperature.

code.title: Expected value, variance and shrinking standard error
code.python:
import random, math

faces = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
mean = sum(faces) / 6
var = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in faces) / 6
print("die mean =", mean, " variance =", round(var, 4), " std =", round(math.sqrt(var), 4))

random.seed(1)
for n in (10, 100, 10000):
    rolls = [random.choice(faces) for _ in range(n)]
    avg = sum(rolls) / n
    se = math.sqrt(var) / math.sqrt(n)      # standard error = sigma / sqrt(n)
    print("n =", n, " sample mean =", round(avg, 3), " std error =", round(se, 3))

# Accuracy of a 100-example test: p=0.8
p, n = 0.8, 100
print("accuracy std error =", round(math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n), 3))
print("4x data (n=400)    =", round(math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / 400), 3))

followUps:
Because the sample mean is measured around itself, not the true mean, so the squared deviations come out a bit too small. Dividing by n-1 corrects that.

Take [1,3]: sample mean 2, squared deviations sum to 2. Dividing by n=2 gives 1, by n-1=1 gives 2. This is Bessel's correction and it makes the estimator unbiased. For n=100 the difference is 1%, so it matters mostly for small samples.

Then the average may not settle down, or it converges far more slowly than 1/sqrt(n), so the usual confidence statements fail.

The Cauchy distribution has no mean at all: the average of a million samples is no more stable than a single sample. Heavy-tailed data like income or latency can behave this way in practice. I use the median, trimmed means or quantiles, and look at the tail rather than trusting the mean.

Big enough that the standard error is smaller than the differences you care about. Roughly n = p(1-p)/SE^2.

For accuracy near 80% and a wanted standard error of 1 point (0.01): n = 0.8x0.2/0.0001 = 1,600. For 0.5 points you need 6,400 (4x data halves the error). To compare two models you need a paired test on the same examples, and the set must also represent real traffic, including rare classes.

code.title: Shapes in attention scoring with a causal mask
code.python:
import math

def matmul(A, B):
    return [[sum(a * b for a, b in zip(r, c)) for c in zip(*B)] for r in A]

def shape(M):
    return (len(M), len(M[0]))

def softmax_row(r):
    m = max(r)
    e = [math.exp(x - m) for x in r]
    return [x / sum(e) for x in e]

n, d = 3, 2
Q = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]
K = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]
V = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]       # values, shape (n, d_v)
Kt = [list(c) for c in zip(*K)]
scores = matmul(Q, Kt)
print("Q", shape(Q), "K^T", shape(Kt), "-> scores", shape(scores))
scaled = [[x / math.sqrt(d) for x in r] for r in scores]
mask = [[x if j <= i else -1e9 for j, x in enumerate(r)] for i, r in enumerate(scaled)]
w = [softmax_row(r) for r in mask]          # each row sums to 1; causal mask
for r in w:
    print([round(x, 3) for x in r], "sum =", round(sum(r), 3))
out = matmul(w, V)
print("weights", shape(w), "x V", shape(V), "-> output", shape(out))
print("n x n entries:", n * n, "; for n = 4096 it is", 4096 * 4096)

followUps:
It stops each token from looking at later tokens, which is needed for next-token prediction. The model must not see the answer it is predicting.

Before softmax you set scores for positions j > i to a large negative number (such as -1e9), so their weights become 0. For n=3, row 0 can use only token 0, row 1 tokens 0-1, row 2 tokens 0-2. The weight matrix is lower triangular, and each row still sums to 1.

Each head works on a smaller slice of the width, and the head outputs are concatenated back to the full width.

With d_model=512 and 8 heads, each head has d_k=64. Per head Q, K, V are (n, 64), scores are (n, n), output is (n, 64). Concatenating 8 heads gives (n, 512), then a final (512, 512) projection. Total compute is similar to one big head, but there are 8 separate n x n score matrices.

It computes attention in small tiles and keeps running softmax statistics, so the full n x n matrix is never written to slow GPU memory.

For each block of queries it loops over blocks of keys and values, updating a running max and sum so the softmax stays exact. Memory drops from O(n^2) to O(n), and it is faster because it avoids moving a huge matrix between memory levels. The result is identical, not an approximation.

code.title: Impute with train median plus a missing flag
code.python:
import statistics

train = [30, None, 50, 40, None, 200]
test = [None, 45]
known = [x for x in train if x is not None]
print("train:", train, " test:", test)
print("mean(known) =", statistics.mean(known), " median(known) =", statistics.median(known))

def impute(xs, fill):
    # keep a "was missing" flag because missingness can be informative
    return [fill if x is None else x for x in xs], [int(x is None) for x in xs]

fill = statistics.median(known)      # learned from TRAIN only
t_vals, t_flag = impute(train, fill)
s_vals, s_flag = impute(test, fill)  # reuse the same fill at inference
print("train filled:", t_vals, t_flag)
print("test  filled:", s_vals, s_flag)
print("missing fraction:", round(sum(t_flag) / len(train), 2))
# Sentinel trap: -1 treated as a real number drags the mean down
bad = [30, -1, 50]
print("mean with sentinel:", round(statistics.mean(bad), 2), "vs true:", statistics.mean([30, 50]))

followUps:
MCAR means missing completely at random, MAR means missing at random given other columns, MNAR means missing not at random.

MCAR: a sensor dropped readings by chance, so dropping rows is safe. MAR: older users skip a field, so missingness depends on age, which you can model. MNAR: high earners hide their income, so the missing value itself explains why it is missing and any simple fill is biased. The type decides which fix is acceptable.

Drop rows when very few are affected and the missing ones are random, or drop a column when most of it is missing and it carries little signal.

If 0.5% of 1,000,000 rows have a missing value, dropping them loses almost nothing. If 70% of a column is empty, filling it mostly invents data. Do not drop if missingness is itself informative or tied to a class, because you will distort the sample.

XGBoost learns a default direction for missing values at every split, so you do not have to fill them.

During training, for each split it tries sending the missing rows left and right, and keeps whichever lowers the loss more. At prediction time the same learned direction is used. This works well when missingness has meaning, but you still need to check that missing rate in production resembles training.

I would test the properties of the output, not individual lines: row counts, shapes, no unexpected NaN, and values on a case I can compute by hand.

Examples: a 3-row sample whose group averages I calculate on paper; an empty input; a column with all NaN; duplicate keys; and a comparison against a slow pure-Python version on random data. Assertions like assert out.shape == (n, d) and a train/test leak check catch the common mistakes cheaply.

Anything personal, confidential or that you are not allowed to share: customer records, credentials and keys, internal code or business numbers.

Instead share the schema, column names with fake values, or a synthetic sample with the same shape. For instance, replace real names and emails with generated ones and keep the data types and edge cases. Always follow company policy and check whether the tool keeps or trains on what you send.

When I cannot verify it, when it touches security or money in a way I do not understand, or when policy forbids it.

If I cannot explain each line, or I cannot test it on data with a known answer, I will not ship it. Likewise for code that handles credentials or personal data, or copied code with an unclear licence. In those cases I write it myself or ask a colleague to review.
